Desired settings in a task are validated when the task is saved: unknown keys are rejected so a typo cannot silently do nothing.

With Manage index settings on, a task owns the settings it declares: When the task starts, the live settings are compared with the desired ones and only the differences are applied (applying 3 changed index settings in the log). The task's Index settings tab shows desired versus live values, highlights drift (someone changed the index by hand, or a deployment changed the task), and applies the desired settings with one click. Only keys present in the desired settings are compared, so settings the task does not manage never show up as drift. Lists whose order does not matter (filterable and sortable attributes, for example) are compared as sets. If Meilisearch rejects the update when the task starts, the start fails with Meilisearch's message (apply settings: …) and the task keeps retrying with backoff until the settings are fixed. Desired settings that cannot be parsed fail the task outright.

When a task starts, it makes sure its index uses the task's primary key field: A missing index is created with that primary key. An empty index with another primary key is switched to it. An index that has documents and another primary key is refused, and the task fails: index "products" uses "sku" but the task writes "id" and the index holds 1200 documents; use a new index, change mapping.primaryKeyField, or resync with zero-downtime enabled. A zero-downtime resync builds a fresh shadow index with the new key and swaps it in.

The task queue, dumps, snapshots and experimental features belong to a whole Meilisearch instance and live on the destination's page; see per-instance pages. The top-level Meilisearch tasks page shows the task queue of every instance. The Meilisearch task queue, per instance.

Check that Meilisearch matches the source: schema check, document diff and repair, and the dead letter queue with replay and discard. Three tools tell you whether an index really matches its source: the schema check, the document diff (with repair), and the dead letter queue of documents Meilisearch refused.

The Schema check tab of a task (any role) compares three things: the source's columns, the fields actually present in the index (with their coverage, the share of documents that have the field), and the index settings. Each field shows where it comes from, its source type, whether it is in the source and in the index, and which settings reference it (searchable, displayed, filterable, sortable, distinct, ranking). The schema check with issues sorted by severity. Issues it reports: Level Issue error index primary key is "sku" but the task writes "id" error the source has no primary key; set mapping.primaryKey error settings reference filterable but no document can contain it (a setting names a field the mapping never produces) warning field exists in the index but not in the source (dropped or renamed column?); a zero-downtime resync removes it warning date stored as RFC3339 text cannot be range filtered or sorted chronologically; set mapping.timeFormat to unix warning some documents miss the primary key field info column is mapped but no indexed document has it yet info binary column is indexed as base64 text; consider excluding it info add _geo to filterable/sortable attributes to use geo search info the index does not exist yet; it is created when the task starts

The Diff tab (moderator to run) compares the source and the index document by document: Source pass. Reads every row with the task's own snapshot query, applies the mapping, and keeps a hash of each document. Index pass. Pages through every document in the index and compares hashes. Detail pass. Re-reads the source for sample documents to show which fields differ, and for repairs. The report counts documents in the source and the index and the missing (in the source, not in the index), extra (in the index, not in the source) and mismatched (different content) ones, with up to 50 sample ids per category (sampleLimit) and, for mismatches, the differing fields with both values. Floats are compared to 15 significant digits, because Meilisearch does not keep the last digit of some floats; without this, documents that are in sync would never compare equal. A diff runs in the background (at most one per task, for at most two hours) and the report is kept until the next run. It reads the whole table, so schedule large diffs outside peak hours. Memory grows with the number of documents (one hash per document).

Repair runs the diff again and fixes the index while it goes, for the categories you choose: re-send missing and mismatched documents, and delete extra ones. Deleting extras is off by default: check the sample ids first, in case another task writes to the same index. Documents Meilisearch rejects during a repair go to the dead letter queue. The log records repair: 12 upserted, 3 deleted, 0 rejected. # API: run a diff, then read the report curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sampleLimit": 50, "compareFields": true}' "$CDC/api/v1/tasks/products/diff" curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$CDC/api/v1/tasks/products/diff" # Repair missing and mismatched documents (runs in the background as well) curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"missing": true, "mismatched": true, "extra": false}' "$CDC/api/v1/tasks/products/diff/repair" Diff versus resync A repair fixes a handful of documents without rebuilding anything. When most of the index is wrong (after a mapping change, say), a zero-downtime Resync is faster and cleaner.

When Meilisearch refuses a batch because of a document's content, the writer splits the batch in halves until it isolates the offending documents. Everything else is applied; the offenders are stored in the task's dead letter queue (DLQ) with the error, the Meilisearch error code and the number of attempts. The pipeline keeps going. Dead letters with the reason Meilisearch gave.

Operation Typical cause upsert, replace, delete Meilisearch rejected the document: an invalid or missing document id, a malformed _geo or GeoJSON field, the per-document field limit, an invalid _vectors value, a malformed payload, or a single document too large for the payload limit. transform The row could not become a document at all, usually because a primary key column has no value (row has no value for a primary key column "id"). The original row is stored.

Replay (moderator) sends the selected entries (or all) to Meilisearch again, after you fixed the cause (for example by adjusting index settings or embedders). Entries that succeed leave the queue; the others stay with their attempt count increased. transform entries cannot be replayed: fix the source row or the mapping, and the next change of that row is applied normally. Discard (moderator) deletes the selected entries (or all). Dead letters are kept in the state store until replayed, discarded, the task is deleted, or purged with meilisearch-cdc admin purge dlq. The cdc_dlq_total metric and the dlq alert rule tell you when new ones arrive.

Monitor meilisearch-cdc: the live dashboard, Server-Sent Events, Prometheus metrics with names and labels, health endpoints and logs. Watch pipelines live in the dashboard, scrape Prometheus metrics, probe health endpoints and ship structured logs.

The Overview page shows the tasks by state, the combined throughput (events per second across all tasks), documents written, firing alerts, dead letters, snapshot progress, each Meilisearch destination's health, and a feed of recent activity. Every page updates live; the top bar shows Live while the event stream is connected and reconnects by itself. The overview page.

The dashboard is fed by GET /api/v1/events, a Server-Sent Events stream you can also consume yourself. It needs authentication; because EventSource cannot set headers, this endpoint also accepts the admin token as ?token=. Event Data When status A task status (state, counters, lag, rate, checkpoint…) On every change, at most about twice per second per task; one per task when the stream opens. log A task log entry {"time","taskId","level","message"} As it happens. task {"id","action"} with created, updated, deleted or diff When the task list changes or a diff finishes. overview The same object as GET /api/v1/overview When the stream opens, then every 2 seconds. destination.health {"id","health"} After each destination health check. alert An alert event When an alert fires, repeats or resolves. curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/events # retry: 3000 # # event: overview # data: {"tasks":{"total":3,"byState":{"streaming":3}}, ...} Behind a reverse proxy, disable response buffering for this path; see Reverse proxy and TLS.

Metrics are served at /metrics (not under /api) in the Prometheus text format. The endpoint requires authentication: use the static admin token (CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN) as a bearer token. # prometheus.yml scrape_configs: - job_name: meilisearch-cdc metrics_path: /metrics authorization: type: Bearer credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/cdc-admin-token static_configs: - targets: ["cdc.internal:8080"] Metric Type Labels Meaning cdc_events_total counter task, op (upsert, delete, truncate) Change events read from sources (snapshot rows count as upserts). cdc_documents_total counter task, kind (upserted, deleted) Documents confirmed by Meilisearch. cdc_batches_total counter task Batches confirmed by Meilisearch. cdc_batch_duration_seconds histogram task Time from enqueueing a batch to its confirmation. Buckets from 10 ms doubling to about 20 s. cdc_errors_total counter task Pipeline failures (each restart and each configuration failure). cdc_retries_total counter task Retried Meilisearch operations. cdc_dlq_total counter task Documents sent to the dead letter queue. cdc_lag_seconds gauge task Delay between the source commit and the Meilisearch confirmation of the last batch. cdc_inflight_batches gauge task Batches enqueued but not yet confirmed. cdc_task_running gauge task 1 while the task's pipeline is active, 0 when it stopped. The task label is the task id. Series of a deleted task are removed. The standard Go runtime (go_*) and process (process_*) collectors are included. Counters start at zero when the service starts.

# Documents per second, per task sum by (task) (rate(cdc_documents_total[5m])) # Tasks lagging more than a minute max by (task) (cdc_lag_seconds) > 60 # 95th percentile batch confirmation time histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, task) (rate(cdc_batch_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) # New dead letters in the last hour increase(cdc_dlq_total[1h]) > 0

Endpoint Auth Response GET /healthz none ok while the HTTP server runs. Use it for liveness and readiness probes. GET /api/v1/health none {"status":"ok","meilisearch":{"status":"available","version":"…","destination":"…"}}; the status is unavailable (with error) when the default destination does not answer within 3 seconds, and unconfigured when there is no destination. GET /api/v1/overview viewer Task counts by state, total counters, rate, the default instance and every destination's health, and the registered source types. GET /api/v1/tasks/{id}/metrics viewer The task's rate, lag, upserted and deleted counts over about the last ten minutes at 2-second resolution, and its checkpoint.

Service logs go to standard error, as text or JSON (CDC_LOG_FORMAT), at the level of CDC_LOG_LEVEL. Each task also keeps its last 1,000 activity entries in memory, visible on its Logs tab and in the log events. See Logging.
For notifications instead of dashboards, define alert rules: task state, lag, dead letters, error bursts, stalled snapshots and Meilisearch down, delivered by email, Telegram or webhook.

Alert rules (task state, lag, dead letters, errors, stalled, Meilisearch down) delivered by email (SMTP), Telegram or webhook. Alert rules watch tasks and Meilisearch instances and notify you by email, Telegram or webhook when something needs attention, then again when it is resolved. Rules, firing alerts and the delivery history.

A rule can only be created or enabled when email (SMTP) or a Telegram bot is configured (otherwise 409: alerts need a notification channel). Every rule needs at least one recipient: an email address, a Telegram chat or a webhook URL. Email recipients need SMTP and Telegram chats need the bot (422 with the reason). A disabled rule can always be saved. Managing rules needs the admin role; viewing them, the history and active alerts needs viewer.

Type Fires when Parameters (defaults) task_state A task is in one of the chosen states. states (failed, held; retrying and others can be added) lag A streaming task's lag exceeds the threshold. thresholdMs, required (the dashboard asks for seconds) dlq At least count new dead letters arrived within the window. count (1), window (5m) errors At least count pipeline errors happened within the window. count (1), window (5m) stalled A task in starting, snapshotting, resyncing or retrying made no progress for the for duration. for (10m) meili_down A Meilisearch destination is unhealthy. destinationIds (empty = every destination)

Field Default Meaning name required Shown in notifications. enabled Disabled rules are not evaluated. taskIds empty = every task The tasks the rule watches (ignored by meili_down). condition.for 0 How long the condition must hold before the alert fires (all types; stalled already includes it). severity warning info, warning or critical. cooldown 30m While an alert keeps firing, a reminder is sent after each cooldown. At least 1m. notifyResolved off Also notify when the condition clears. channels emails, telegramChatIds, webhookUrl, webhookSecret. Rules are evaluated every CDC_ALERT_INTERVAL (5 seconds by default), separately for each task (or destination). Alert state is persisted, so a restart does not send the same notification again. Changing a rule restarts its state. { "name": "Pipeline failed or held", "enabled": true, "condition": {"type": "task_state", "states": ["failed", "held"], "for": "1m"}, "taskIds": [], "severity": "critical", "channels": { "emails": ["ops@example.com"], "telegramChatIds": ["-1001234567890"], "webhookUrl": "https://hooks.example.com/cdc", "webhookSecret": "whsec_…" }, "cooldown": "30m", "notifyResolved": true }

Send test on a rule delivers a test notification (marked TEST) on each of its channels and shows each delivery's result. Test notifications are not stored. The history lists every firing, reminder and resolution with each delivery (channel, target, success or error), filterable by rule and state. Active alerts are the ones firing now; they also appear live in the dashboard.

Configure it in Settings → Email (admin). Email is also used for invitations and password resets. SMTP settings with a test email. Field Meaning Host, port The SMTP server. Port 465 for TLS, 587 for STARTTLS, 25 for a local relay. An empty host disables email. Encryption auto (default): TLS from the first byte on port 465, STARTTLS otherwise, and plain text only when the server lacks STARTTLS and no password is sent. tls: TLS from the first byte. starttls: upgrade a plain connection. none: plain text, for local relays only. Username, password Optional. The password is stored encrypted and shown masked. From The sender address, for example Meili CDC <cdc@example.com>. Public URL The dashboard URL used in links (overrides CDC_PUBLIC_URL). A mode that cannot work on its port is corrected when sending: starttls on port 465 uses TLS, and tls on ports 25 or 587 uses STARTTLS. If a password would be sent over a server without STARTTLS, sending fails rather than leaking it. Send test email reports the server's answer; typical errors explain the port and mode mismatch, for example the server sent no greeting: it probably expects TLS from the start; use port 465 with TLS, or check the port.

Configure it in Settings → Telegram (admin): In Telegram, talk to @BotFather and send /newbot. Copy the token it gives you. Paste the token and save. The service validates it with the Bot API's getMe (an invalid token is refused with 422) and shows the bot's name. The token is stored encrypted. Add the bot to your group, or to your channel as an administrator, then send a message there. Find the chat id: open https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/getUpdates and read chat.id. Group and channel ids start with -100; a public channel can also be addressed as @channelname. Send a test message from the settings page, then use the id in alert rules. The API URL defaults to https://api.telegram.org and can point to a self-hosted Bot API server. Telegram messages are sent as HTML with a link to the dashboard when a public URL is known; Telegram's flood control (retry_after) is honoured.

A rule with a webhookUrl POSTs a JSON body to it. The text field makes Slack, Mattermost and Discord-compatible endpoints render the alert directly: { "text": "[CRITICAL] Pipeline failed or held · Products\nTask \"Products\" is failed: open source: postgres: connect: …", "link": "https://cdc.example.com/#/tasks/products", "event": { "id": "00000001761500000000-a1b2c3d4", "ruleId": "r1", "ruleName": "Pipeline failed or held", "severity": "critical", "taskId": "products", "taskName": "Products", "state": "firing", "message": "Task \"Products\" is failed: open source: postgres: connect: …", "at": "2026-10-26T20:12:00Z", "deliveries": [] } } The subject line in text is [LABEL] rule name · task or destination name, where the label is the severity in capitals, RESOLVED for resolutions and starts with TEST · for test sends. event may also carry destinationId, destinationName and reminder: true. link is empty when no public URL is known. Delivery is tried up to 3 times within 30 seconds; 429 and 5xx are retried, other 4xx responses are not.

Give the rule a signing secret (channels.webhookSecret, at least 16 characters; Generate creates a whsec_… value, and it requires a webhook URL). Every delivery then carries the same two headers the webhook source uses: X-CDC-Timestamp: 1767225600 X-CDC-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + raw body)> The secret is encrypted at rest and returned as ••••••; send the mask back to keep it. Receivers should recompute the HMAC over the raw body bytes (before any JSON parsing), compare it in constant time, and reject timestamps older than a few minutes to block replays. Verify in Node.js import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto'; import express from 'express'; const SECRET = process.env.CDC_ALERT_SECRET; const app = express(); app.post('/cdc', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => { const ts = req.get('X-CDC-Timestamp') || ''; const got = Buffer.from(req.get('X-CDC-Signature') || ''); const want = Buffer.from('sha256=' + createHmac('sha256', SECRET).update(`${ts}.`).update(req.body).digest('hex')); const fresh = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(ts)) <= 300; if (!fresh || got.length !== want.length || !timingSafeEqual(got, want)) return res.sendStatus(401); const alert = JSON.parse(req.body); console.log(alert.text); res.sendStatus(204); }); app.listen(3000); Verify in Python import hashlib, hmac, os, time from flask import Flask, request, abort SECRET = os.environ["CDC_ALERT_SECRET"].encode() app = Flask(__name__) @app.post("/cdc") def cdc_alert(): ts = request.headers.get("X-CDC-Timestamp", "") sig = request.headers.get("X-CDC-Signature", "") body = request.get_data() # raw bytes want = "sha256=" + hmac.new(SECRET, ts.encode() + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest() if not ts.isdigit() or abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > 300 or not hmac.compare_digest(sig, want): abort(401) print(request.get_json()["text"]) return "", 204 To test a receiver by hand, compute a signature with openssl exactly as in the webhook source example.

Roles and the permission matrix, invitations, password reset, the primary administrator, sessions, CSRF, rate limiting, audit log and secret encryption. Accounts with three roles, an owner who cannot be locked out, server-side sessions with CSRF protection, brute-force limits, an audit log, and credentials encrypted at rest.

Role Can viewer Read everything except users, invitations, SMTP and Telegram settings, MCP settings and tokens, the task export and the audit log. Search indexes and preview settings. moderator Viewer, plus operate existing tasks: start, stop, pause, resume, restart, resync, reset checkpoint (one or in batch), run diffs and repairs, replay and discard dead letters, test task definitions, push to webhook tasks, cancel Meilisearch tasks, run destination health checks. admin Everything: create, edit, delete, import and export tasks; connectors and destinations; index changes (create, delete, settings, primary key, swap, compact); dumps, snapshots and experimental features; users and invitations; SMTP and Telegram; alert rules; MCP; the audit log. Members, roles and pending invitations.

The server enforces a role per API route. Routes not listed below need viewer for GET and admin for everything else, so new routes are locked down by default. The dashboard hides or disables what your role cannot do, and the server answers 403 {"error":"requires role moderator"} if you try anyway. Public routes (no authentication): GET /health, GET /auth/config, POST /auth/setup, /auth/login, /auth/logout, /auth/forgot, /auth/reset, GET /auth/invite/{token}, POST /auth/invite/accept, plus /healthz outside the API.

Invite (Settings → Users, admin): enter an email and a role. The invitation link is valid for 7 days and works once. With SMTP configured it is emailed; otherwise (or as well) the link is shown once so you can send it yourself. The invitee chooses a name and password and is signed in. Create directly: an admin can create an account with a password (API POST /api/v1/users), or on the server with meilisearch-cdc admin users create. Passwords have 8 to 128 characters and are hashed with argon2id.

Forgot password appears on the sign-in page only when SMTP is configured. It always answers the same way, whether or not the email exists, and emails a link valid for one hour. Using it sets the new password and signs the user out of other sessions. An admin can set another user's password (that user's sessions are revoked), except the primary administrator's. Each user can change their own password from the user menu (other sessions are revoked). Without email, and for the primary administrator, use the CLI: meilisearch-cdc admin users reset-password --email … --generate. See recovery recipes.

The first admin (created by the setup page or CDC_ADMIN_EMAIL) is the primary administrator, or owner. On data from an older version, the oldest admin becomes the owner at startup. In the dashboard and the API, for every caller, the admin token included: nobody can change their own role; nobody can change the owner's role or delete the owner (403); only the owner can set the owner's password; the last admin cannot be demoted or deleted (409), and you cannot delete yourself. Only the server CLI transfers ownership (admin users set-owner, to another admin) or resets the owner's password. To demote or delete the owner, transfer ownership first.

Signing in creates a server-side session and sets the cookie cdc_session (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/). It is Secure on HTTPS, behind a proxy that sends X-Forwarded-Proto: https with CDC_TRUST_PROXY, or always with CDC_COOKIE_SECURE. Sessions last 7 days and slide: activity extends them. Signing out revokes the session. Cookie-authenticated writes (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) must come from the same origin: the Origin header (or Referer) must match the request's host, otherwise 403 cross-origin request refused. Browsers send it automatically; bearer-token requests are not subject to it. Admins can sign everyone out with meilisearch-cdc admin sessions revoke.

What Limit Failed sign-ins per client IP 30 per 15 minutes Failed sign-ins per account (email) 10 per 15 minutes; a successful sign-in resets it Forgot password requests per IP count against the same IP limit, success or not Wrong current password when changing one's own password 10 per 15 minutes per user A blocked request gets 429 with a Retry-After header and {"error":"too many attempts, try again later","retryAfter":n}. Behind a proxy, enable CDC_TRUST_PROXY so the limit applies to the real client IP.

Settings → Audit log (admin) lists, newest first, who did what, when and from which IP: sign-ins (auth.login), failed sign-ins (auth.login_failed), setup, invitation acceptance, reset requests and password resets; every successful write through the API or the dashboard, recorded with the route as its action (for example POST /api/v1/tasks/{id}/{action}) and the path as its target; every mutating MCP tool call (mcp.<tool>, with its arguments); every CLI command, refused ones included (cli.<command>, user cli). Passwords are never recorded. The most recent 20,000 entries are kept. API: GET /api/v1/audit?limit=200.

CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN (or CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN_FILE) defines one bearer token with the admin role, for scripts, CI, Prometheus and webhook pushers. It acts as a user named API token; the dashboard's sign-in page also offers Use an API token instead. The service keeps only its hash in memory. Rotate it by changing the variable and restarting. Generate a long random value: openssl rand -hex 32 curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN" https://cdc.example.com/api/v1/tasks AI agents get their own revocable, role-scoped tokens instead; see MCP.

Connector passwords (in connection strings), DynamoDB secret keys, Meilisearch API keys, the SMTP password, the Telegram bot token and webhook signing secrets are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before they are stored. Each ciphertext is bound to its record and field (associated data such as task:<id>:dsn or destination:<id>:apiKey), so a value copied into another record cannot be decrypted there. Secrets stay encrypted in memory and are decrypted only when a connection is opened. The API never returns them: they come back as ••••••, and sending the mask back keeps the stored value. The key is CDC_SECRET_KEY (a base64 string of exactly 32 bytes is used directly, anything else is a passphrase stretched with argon2id), or, when it is unset, a random key generated once in <data-dir>/secret.key (mode 0600). Setting CDC_SECRET_KEY later makes the service ignore secret.key, so rotate as below rather than just switching. Passwords of user accounts are not encrypted but hashed (argon2id); MCP tokens and the admin token are stored or held as hashes.

The service holds a key ring: the current key encrypts, and CDC_SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS can still decrypt. At startup every secret still encrypted with the previous key (or stored in an older format, or in plain text) is re-encrypted with the current one. Generate a new key: openssl rand -base64 32. Set CDC_SECRET_KEY to the new key and CDC_SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS to the old one. If the old key was the generated file, use its content: CDC_SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS="$(cat /var/lib/meilisearch-cdc/secret.key)". Restart. The log shows re-encrypted stored secrets with the current key for tasks and connectors; destinations and notification settings are re-encrypted as they load. Check that tasks run and connectors test fine, take a backup, then remove CDC_SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS and restart again. Only one previous key is supported at a time. A value encrypted with a key that is not configured fails with value was encrypted with a key that is not configured (set CDC_SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS). Give the admin CLI the same key variables as the service.

Let AI assistants manage meilisearch-cdc over the Model Context Protocol: enable /mcp, create tokens, configure clients, tools, resources and policy. meilisearch-cdc includes a Model Context Protocol server, so AI assistants and IDE agents can inspect and operate your pipelines with tokens you control, limited to what each role may do. The MCP settings: endpoint, tokens and the access policy.

In Settings → MCP (admin), turn the server on. It speaks MCP's Streamable HTTP transport at /mcp on the service's address, for example https://cdc.example.com/mcp. While disabled, /mcp answers 404. Disabling keeps tokens and the policy; meilisearch-cdc admin mcp disable does the same from the server.

Every client authenticates with its own bearer token: Authorization: Bearer cdcmcp_…. Generate token: a name (where it is used, such as "Claude Desktop (ops)"), a role (viewer, moderator or admin) and an expiry (never, 7, 30 or 90 days in the dashboard; any duration such as "720h" through the API). The token is shown once, together with a ready-to-paste client configuration. Only a hash is stored; the list shows its prefix (cdcmcp_ab12), creator, last use and expiry. Rotate issues a new token with the same name, role and lifetime; the old one stops working at once. Revoke deletes it. Revocation, expiry and policy changes apply to the very next call, even in an open session. meilisearch-cdc admin mcp revoke-tokens revokes them all from the server.

This is the snippet the dashboard shows when a token is created; most MCP clients that support remote HTTP servers accept this shape: { "mcpServers": { "meilisearch-cdc": { "type": "http", "url": "https://cdc.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer cdcmcp_…" } } } }
claude mcp add --transport http meilisearch-cdc https://cdc.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer cdcmcp_…"

Claude Desktop's configuration file starts local (stdio) servers. Bridge to the remote endpoint with the mcp-remote package (needs Node.js), in claude_desktop_config.json: { "mcpServers": { "meilisearch-cdc": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://cdc.example.com/mcp", "--header", "Authorization: Bearer ${CDC_MCP_TOKEN}"], "env": { "CDC_MCP_TOKEN": "cdcmcp_…" } } } } Clients must reach the endpoint over HTTPS in production; see Reverse proxy and TLS (the /mcp path should not be buffered).

The minimum role is the default grant; the policy can change it. Mutating tools are marked as such to clients (destructive hint) and every successful mutating call is written to the audit log as mcp.<tool> with its arguments. Tool Min. role Mutating What it does overview viewer no Summary of all tasks, throughput and the Meilisearch instance. list_tasks viewer no CDC tasks with their live status (secrets redacted). get_task viewer no A task definition and its live status, counters, lag and checkpoint. get_task_logs viewer no Recent activity log of a task, newest last. schema_check viewer no Compare source columns, index fields and index settings; lists issues. get_diff viewer no The last document diff between source and index. list_dlq viewer no Documents Meilisearch rejected for a task. list_destinations viewer no Meilisearch instances with health, last sync and the tasks writing to them. list_indexes viewer no Indexes with document counts and the tasks writing them. get_index viewer no Index primary key, stats and field distribution. search_index viewer no Run a Meilisearch search to verify synced data. get_index_settings viewer no Current Meilisearch settings of an index. preview_index_settings viewer no Which settings would change, without applying them. list_meili_tasks viewer no Recent Meilisearch tasks (custom metadata cdc:<task> marks CDC writes). list_alert_rules viewer no Alert rules and their channels. list_alert_events viewer no Recent alert events, newest first. task_action moderator yes Start, stop, pause, resume, restart, resync or reset the checkpoint of a task. batch_task_action moderator yes Apply a lifecycle action to several tasks. test_connection moderator no Connect with a task definition, read its schema and sample documents. run_diff moderator yes Start a document diff (and optional repair); poll get_diff. replay_dlq moderator yes Resend rejected documents to Meilisearch. create_task admin yes Create a task from a definition (see the cdc://docs/api resource). update_task admin yes Replace a task definition; running tasks restart. delete_task admin yes Delete a task, optionally with its source resources and index. update_index_settings admin yes Apply Meilisearch settings to an index and wait for the task. create_alert_rule admin yes Create an alert rule with email, Telegram or webhook channels. delete_alert_rule admin yes Delete an alert rule. Index tools accept an optional destination argument (the default destination when omitted).

URI Content cdc://overview Tasks by state, throughput and Meilisearch health. cdc://tasks Every task with its status. cdc://tasks/{id} One task with its status. cdc://tasks/{id}/logs Recent activity of a task. cdc://indexes Indexes of the default Meilisearch destination. cdc://destinations Destinations with health and synced tasks. cdc://alerts/active Alerts currently firing. cdc://docs/api The REST API and the task and rule JSON formats, for agents that create tasks.

The policy grants each role a list of tools and resources. By default every role gets the tools whose minimum role it meets and every resource. Admins can tick or untick tools and resources per role in the MCP tab, and Reset to defaults restores the default grants. A session sees only the tools and resources its token's role is granted, and every call is checked again against the current policy. Grant carefully The policy is the check MCP calls go through: granting an admin tool such as delete_task to the viewer role lets viewer tokens use it. Keep mutating tools on roles whose tokens you would trust with them.

Mutating calls appear in Settings → Audit log as mcp.task_action, mcp.create_task, … with the token's name (mcp:<name>) and up to 500 characters of the arguments. Token creation, rotation, revocation and policy changes are recorded like any other admin write.

The meilisearch-cdc admin operator CLI: users, sessions, MCP and purge commands, socket and direct modes, and recovery recipes. meilisearch-cdc admin is the operator CLI, run on the server: recover accounts, transfer the primary administrator, sign everyone out, turn MCP off, and purge stored data. It uses the same binary as the service. The admin CLI in a terminal.

$ meilisearch-cdc admin --help Usage: meilisearch-cdc admin [config flags] <command> [flags] Operator commands, run on the server. They go through the running service (its admin socket <data-dir>/admin.sock) or, while it is stopped, work on the data directory directly. Every command is recorded in the audit log with the actor "cli". Commands: users list list accounts users create add an account users reset-password set a new password and sign the user out everywhere users set-role change an account's role users set-owner make an admin the primary administrator users delete delete an account and its sessions sessions revoke sign one user, or everyone, out mcp disable turn the MCP server off (tokens and policy stay) mcp revoke-tokens revoke every MCP token purge <scope>... permanently delete stored data Config flags are the service's own, with the same environment variables, so the CLI finds the same data directory and key: -data-dir (CDC_DATA_DIR), -secret-key (CDC_SECRET_KEY), -meili-url (MEILI_URL), ... -json print machine readable JSON Run "meilisearch-cdc admin <command> --help" for a command's flags. Config flags go before the command; -json may go before or after it. The exit code is 0 on success, 1 when the command failed and 2 for usage errors. meilisearch-cdc without admin runs the service.

Situation What happens The service is running The CLI sends the command to the service's Unix socket <data-dir>/admin.sock (mode 0600, removed on shutdown), and the running service applies it: a purge stops the affected tasks cleanly and dashboards see the change at once. File permissions are the authorization: whoever can open the socket can read the data directory anyway. The service is stopped The CLI opens cdc.db itself and runs the same code. The database is locked but nothing answers on the socket The CLI stops with … is locked by a running service that does not answer on … (an older version, or the socket could not be created; see its log): stop the service and retry. The CLI reads the service's configuration (flags and environment variables), so give it the same CDC_DATA_DIR, and the same CDC_SECRET_KEY if the service does not use the generated secret.key. Without a key it refuses to open the data directory, and without a database it says no database at data/cdc.db: check -data-dir (CDC_DATA_DIR); the service must have started once. CDC_DATA_DIR=/var/lib/meilisearch-cdc meilisearch-cdc admin users list CDC_SECRET_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/cdc-key meilisearch-cdc admin -data-dir /var/lib/meilisearch-cdc users list docker exec -it cdc meilisearch-cdc admin users list kubectl -n cdc exec -it deploy/meilisearch-cdc -- meilisearch-cdc admin users list Socket path length Unix socket paths are limited to about 100 characters. With a longer data directory path the service logs admin socket unavailable and runs without it. In our test on macOS the CLI then failed even while the service was stopped (connect to the admin socket …: connect: invalid argument). Keep the data directory path short, or run the CLI from inside the directory: cd /very/long/path && CDC_DATA_DIR=. meilisearch-cdc admin ….

Command Flags What it does users list Accounts, oldest first, with the primary administrator marked. users create --email (required), --name (default: the part of the email before @), --role (viewer by default), password flags Add an account. The first admin of an empty installation becomes the primary administrator. users reset-password --email, password flags Set a new password and sign the user out everywhere. Works for the primary administrator too. users set-role --email, --role (both required) Change a role. The primary administrator's role cannot change, and the last admin cannot be demoted. users set-owner --email Make an admin the primary administrator. users delete --email Delete an account and its sessions. Not the primary administrator, not the last admin. sessions revoke --email (optional) Sign one user out, or everyone without --email. mcp disable Turn the MCP server off; tokens and the policy stay. mcp revoke-tokens Revoke every MCP token. purge <scope>… --yes, --indexes Delete stored data; see Purge. Every command also accepts -json. Passwords for users create and users reset-password (8 to 128 characters): --generate creates a strong random password and prints it once; --password-file F reads it from a file (- for standard input); otherwise, on a terminal, a prompt asks twice without echo; with standard input redirected (and always on Windows), its first line is used.

$ meilisearch-cdc admin users create --help Usage: meilisearch-cdc admin users create [flags] Add an account. Creates an account. The first admin of an empty installation becomes the primary administrator. The password comes from --password-file, --generate, or a prompt (asked twice, not echoed) when stdin is a terminal; otherwise the first line of stdin is used. Passwords have 8 to 128 characters. Flags: -email string the account's email address (required) -generate generate a strong random password and print it once -json print machine readable JSON -name string display name (default: the part of the email before @) -password-file string read the password from this file (- for stdin) -role string viewer, moderator or admin (default "viewer")

Real output (passwords shortened): $ meilisearch-cdc admin users list No users: the dashboard shows the setup page. $ meilisearch-cdc admin users create --email owner@example.com --name Administrator --role admin --generate created owner@example.com (admin) as the primary administrator Generated password (shown only once): AhRWasEcShykjavJ1uBg… $ meilisearch-cdc admin users create --email ops@example.com --role admin --generate created ops@example.com (admin) Generated password (shown only once): goKSegGfcxHwW65dOo7Q… $ meilisearch-cdc admin users create --email viewer@example.com --name Vera --generate created viewer@example.com (viewer) Generated password (shown only once): ArbMHpOz8BY-1ToWQWzu… $ meilisearch-cdc admin users list EMAIL NAME ROLE OWNER LAST SIGN-IN CREATED owner@example.com Administrator admin yes never 2026-10-26 23:42 ops@example.com ops admin never 2026-10-26 23:42 viewer@example.com Vera viewer never 2026-10-26 23:42 $ meilisearch-cdc admin users set-role --email owner@example.com --role viewer error: forbidden: the primary administrator's role cannot be changed; transfer ownership first with `meilisearch-cdc admin users set-owner` $ meilisearch-cdc admin users delete --email owner@example.com error: forbidden: the primary administrator cannot be deleted; transfer ownership first with `meilisearch-cdc admin users set-owner` $ meilisearch-cdc admin users set-owner --email viewer@example.com error: conflict: the primary administrator must be an admin; viewer@example.com is a viewer $ meilisearch-cdc admin users set-owner --email ops@example.com ops@example.com is now the primary administrator $ meilisearch-cdc admin sessions revoke --email viewer@example.com revoked 0 sessions of viewer@example.com $ meilisearch-cdc admin sessions revoke revoked 0 sessions: everyone is signed out $ meilisearch-cdc admin mcp disable the MCP server is disabled; tokens and the policy are kept $ meilisearch-cdc admin mcp revoke-tokens revoked 0 MCP tokens $ printf 'short\n' | meilisearch-cdc admin users reset-password --email viewer@example.com error: password must be 8 to 128 characters $ meilisearch-cdc admin users reset-password --email viewer@example.com --generate reset the password of viewer@example.com and signed them out everywhere Generated password (shown only once): Q-GZlarCaf9cHosL7buK… With -json: { "users": [ { "id": "74e7560236f73f46", "email": "ops@example.com", "name": "ops", "role": "admin", "createdAt": "2026-10-26T20:12:00.239497Z", "updatedAt": "2026-10-26T20:12:00.542017Z", "owner": true } ] } Every command, refused ones included, is recorded in the audit log with the user cli and the action cli.<command>, for example cli.users.reset-password. Passwords never are.

admin purge permanently deletes exactly the data of the scopes you name. It asks you to type purge unless --yes is given. Scopes run in this order: Scope Deletes tasks Every task with its checkpoint, status, dead letters and diff report; running tasks stop first. Meilisearch indexes stay unless --indexes is given, then each task's index is deleted on its destination (a task whose index cannot be deleted is kept and reported). Source resources such as replication slots are not dropped. checkpoints Sync progress: every task runs a full snapshot on its next start. Running tasks restart now. dlq Dead letters of every task. diffs Diff reports; running diffs are cancelled. logs The task activity log. It is kept in memory, so only a running service has one. connectors Saved source connections. Refused while tasks exist, unless tasks is purged in the same command. destinations Meilisearch destinations, with the same rule. With MEILI_URL set, its destination is recreated. alert-rules Alert rules and their alert state; the history stays. alert-events Alert history and alert state; rules stay. mcp-tokens MCP bearer tokens. settings SMTP, Telegram and the MCP settings (MCP is disabled and the default policy applies). sessions Every sign-in session: everyone is signed out. invitations Pending invitations. users Every account with its sessions, invitations and password resets; the next visit shows the setup page (or CDC_ADMIN_EMAIL creates the admin on the next start). audit The audit log. The purge itself is recorded afterwards. all Everything: the data directory is as good as new, except that the secret key file stays. $ meilisearch-cdc admin purge dlq diffs alert-events --yes SCOPE REMOVED dlq 0 diffs 0 alert-events 0 $ meilisearch-cdc admin purge dlq This permanently deletes from /var/lib/meilisearch-cdc: dlq dead letters of every task Type "purge" to confirm: error: purge cancelled: nothing was deleted $ meilisearch-cdc admin purge bogus --yes error: unknown scope "bogus" (tasks, checkpoints, dlq, diffs, logs, connectors, destinations, alert-rules, alert-events, mcp-tokens, settings, sessions, invitations, users, audit or all) Run "meilisearch-cdc admin purge --help" for usage. Purge is not available in the REST API: it is a destructive, server-side operator action.

meilisearch-cdc admin users list # find the email meilisearch-cdc admin users reset-password --email admin@example.com --generate This works for the primary administrator too, and signs the user out everywhere.

Too many failed sign-ins (429): wait 15 minutes, or restart the service, which clears the in-memory rate limits. No admin left you can sign in as: create one with users create --email you@example.com --role admin --generate, or promote an account with users set-role --email you@example.com --role admin. Every session must go (a lost device, a leaked cookie): sessions revoke, then rotate CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN and mcp revoke-tokens if they may be exposed too.

meilisearch-cdc admin users set-role --email new-owner@example.com --role admin # if not admin yet meilisearch-cdc admin users set-owner --email new-owner@example.com meilisearch-cdc admin users set-role --email old-owner@example.com --role viewer # now allowed

meilisearch-cdc admin purge all # asks you to type "purge" meilisearch-cdc admin purge tasks --indexes --yes # tasks and their Meilisearch indexes only After purge all the next visit shows the setup page. Drop replication slots in your databases yourself (see PostgreSQL), since purging does not touch sources. To also discard the encryption key, stop the service and delete the whole data directory instead.

Install the meilisearch-cdc dashboard as an app on desktop or phone, how it behaves offline, and how updates are applied. The dashboard is a progressive web app: it works on phones, can be installed like an app on desktop and mobile, opens instantly from a cached shell, and updates itself when you deploy a new version. The overview on a phone.

Browsers register service workers, and offer installation, only in a secure context: HTTPS, or http://localhost. Behind a TLS proxy (see Reverse proxy and TLS) everything works; on plain HTTP over the network the dashboard still works, without install and offline support. The dashboard must be served at the root of its host name.

Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers (desktop and Android): open the user menu (your initials, top right) and choose Install app. The item appears when the browser offers installation; the browser's own install icon in the address bar works too. Safari on iPhone and iPad: tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. Safari on macOS: File → Add to Dock. The installed app is called Meili CDC, opens on the overview in its own window (standalone display, with window-controls overlay where supported) and offers shortcuts to Tasks, New task and Alerts (long-press or right-click the icon). Sign-in uses the same session cookie as the browser.

The app shell (the page, scripts, styles, icons) is cached, so the app opens even without network. Live data is never cached: /api, /mcp, /metrics, /healthz and /debug always go to the server. While offline, the top bar shows Offline instead of Live, and the dashboard reconnects by itself when the network comes back. Pages are fetched network-first, so an online visit always gets the latest page; static files are served from the cache and refreshed in the background.

Each release embeds a hash of the dashboard's files in its service worker, so a new version gets a new cache and the old one is removed. When a new version is deployed, the app finds it (also each time the tab comes back to the foreground) and shows an Update available notice with a Reload button; the page reloads only after you accept. The service worker and the manifest are served with Cache-Control: no-cache, so browsers see updates at once.

Every page adapts from phone to wide screens: the sidebar collapses behind a menu button, tables reflow to fit narrow screens, and the task wizard shows one step at a time with a progress bar. A task on a phone.

The meilisearch-cdc REST API v1: authentication, errors, tasks, data quality, indexes, destinations, connectors, accounts, alerts and live events. Everything the dashboard does goes through a JSON API under /api/v1. This page covers authentication, errors and every route; the field-level reference is docs/api.md in the repository.

Base path /api/v1; JSON in and out (Content-Type: application/json). Request bodies are limited to 16 MiB (1 MiB on some account routes, 64 MiB for webhook ingest). Durations are strings such as "30s"; times are RFC 3339. Secrets are never returned: they come back as "••••••", and sending the mask back keeps the stored value. Types are defined in internal/model (Task, Status, TaskView, Connector, Destination, DLQEntry, LogEntry, Schema) and internal/diff (Report, SchemaReport).

Method Use Session cookie cdc_session Created by POST /auth/login, /auth/setup or /auth/invite/accept. Valid 7 days, sliding. Cookie-authenticated writes must send an Origin (or Referer) matching the host (CSRF protection); browsers do it automatically. Bearer token Authorization: Bearer $CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN: the static admin token, acting as an admin named "API token". GET /events also accepts ?token=. Webhook signature Only for POST /ingest/{id} on webhook tasks with a signing secret; see Webhook. MCP tokens (cdcmcp_…) authenticate only at /mcp, not at the REST API. The role each route needs is listed in the permission matrix. TOKEN=$CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN CDC=https://cdc.example.com curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$CDC/api/v1/tasks" | jq '.[] | {id, state: .status.state}' # Or sign in and keep the cookie (send Origin on writes) curl -s -c jar -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Origin: $CDC" \ -d '{"email":"you@example.com","password":"…"}' "$CDC/api/v1/auth/login" curl -s -b jar "$CDC/api/v1/auth/me"

Errors are JSON: {"error": "message"}, with details (a list of messages) for validation errors and code when Meilisearch reported the error. Status When 400 Invalid JSON body, unknown batch action, bad parameters, invalid webhook payload. 401 Not authenticated ({"error":"authentication required"}), or an invalid webhook signature. 403 Role too low ({"error":"requires role moderator"}), owner protection, or cross-origin request refused. 404 Unknown task, connector, destination, index or route. 409 Conflict: duplicate id, a resource still in use, a running task writing to an index you delete, a primary key mismatch, a diff already running, single-instance mode, the last admin. 422 Validation failed; details lists every problem, for example ["name is required", "index.uid is required and may only contain a-z A-Z 0-9 - _"]. 429 Too many failed sign-ins; see the Retry-After header. 4xx from Meilisearch Passed through with Meilisearch's message and code (index and instance routes). 503, 504 Webhook ingest: task not running, or confirmation took longer than 60 s.

Route Result GET /health (public) {"status":"ok","meilisearch":{"status":"available","version":"1.x","destination":"…"}} GET /overview Tasks by state, totals, rate, the default instance, every destination, registered source types. GET /events Server-Sent Events; see live events.

Route Notes GET /tasks?state=&q=&tag= [TaskView] (task + status), secrets masked. POST /tasks[?start=true] Body: a task; without id one is generated. 201 TaskView. GET /tasks/{id}, PUT /tasks/{id}, DELETE /tasks/{id}?dropSource=true&deleteIndex=<uid> Update restarts a running task; delete returns 204. POST /tasks/{id}/{action} start, stop, pause, resume, restart, resync, reset-checkpoint. POST /tasks/batch {"ids":[…],"action":"…"} (the actions above except reset-checkpoint, plus delete) → {"results":[{"id","ok","error"}]}. POST /tasks/test Body: a task → {"ok","error","schema","sample":[5 docs],"primaryKey"}. GET /tasks/export, POST /tasks/import Export with secrets masked; import [Task] → {"created":n,"errors":[…]}. GET /tasks/{id}/logs?limit=200 [LogEntry]. GET /tasks/{id}/metrics {"points":[{"t","rate","lagMs","upserted","deleted"}],"checkpoint":{…}}: about 10 minutes at 2 s resolution. GET /tasks/{id}/settings, POST /tasks/{id}/settings/apply Desired versus live index settings and drift; apply the desired settings (admin). POST /ingest/{id} Push changes to a webhook task; see Webhook. # Create a task on a saved connector and start it curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' "$CDC/api/v1/tasks?start=true" -d '{ "id": "products", "name": "Products", "source": {"connectorId": "pg-main", "table": "products"}, "index": {"uid": "products"}, "sync": {"safety": {"maxDeleteRatio": 0.2, "zeroDowntimeResync": true}} }' # Resync it curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$CDC/api/v1/tasks/products/resync"

POST /tasks/{id}/diff {"sampleLimit":50,"compareFields":true} → 202 {"status":"running"}. GET /tasks/{id}/diff The last Report: status, counts, missing, extra, mismatched, inSync, samples, and repair counts when it repaired. Every index and instance route takes ?destination=<id> (the default destination when omitted). Measured meilisearch-cdc throughput, memory sizing, batch size, in-flight batches, gzip, GOMEMLIMIT and GOGC tuning, and profiling with pprof. Meilisearch's own indexing is usually the bottleneck: the service itself uses about a third of one CPU core while feeding tens of thousands of documents per second. Most tuning is about batching.

The numbers come from the load test in test/bench, which runs the real service in-process against real Meilisearch and PostgreSQL containers. They are end to end: a row changes, and the document is confirmed and searchable in Meilisearch. Setup Machine 12-core Apple M-series, containers under OrbStack Source PostgreSQL 17 (postgres:17-alpine): pgoutput replication slot, keyset-paged snapshot copy Destination Meilisearch (getmeili/meilisearch), single node, gzip on Dataset products: 10 columns (bigint id, text name/description/category, numeric price, boolean, text[] tags, jsonb meta, timestamptz, int version) Task settings batchSize 10,000, maxInflight 8, flushInterval 200ms Ranges are the lowest and highest result across repeated runs. Workload Rows Throughput PostgreSQL snapshot (pgoutput slot + keyset copy) 200,000 83k–92k docs/s PostgreSQL streaming (500-row transactions) 50,000 39k–46k docs/s In-memory source snapshot 200,000 64k–73k docs/s In-memory source streaming 50,000 26k–29k docs/s Writer pipeline alone (fake Meilisearch) — ~2.5M docs/s Footprint Value Idle process RSS, dashboard included ~47 MiB Binary size ~55 MiB

Knob Default Effect sync.batchSize 1000 Larger batches mean fewer Meilisearch tasks and better indexing throughput, at the cost of more memory per in-flight batch. 5,000–10,000 suits snapshots. sync.maxInflight 4 Batches waiting for Meilisearch confirmation. Meilisearch auto-batches consecutive tasks, so 8 helps bulk loads. sync.flushInterval 1s Upper bound on how long a change waits in the buffer. Lower it for lower latency on quiet tables. index.writeMode replace upsert (partial update) sends only the fields present, for sources that omit unchanged columns. Destination gzip on Saves bandwidth to remote instances; turn it off on loopback or a LAN to save CPU. GOMEMLIMIT unset Set it to about 80% of the container memory limit, for example GOMEMLIMIT=400MiB. The garbage collector then works harder near the limit instead of the process being killed by the OOM killer. GOGC 100 Raising it (for example 200) trades memory for less GC CPU on busy instances.

Memory scales with batchSize × maxInflight × average document size per running task, plus about 1 MB of logs and metrics history per task. Snapshot reads are chunked (5,000 rows for the SQL sources), and back pressure stops reading from the source while the writer is saturated. Exceptions: the Kafka and Redis snapshots fold the whole topic or stream in memory, and a diff keeps one hash per document while it runs. CPU is mostly garbage collection of short-lived row maps plus network I/O; a fraction of a core per busy task is typical. Disk: cdc.db holds definitions, checkpoints, dead letters, reports, the alert history and up to 20,000 audit entries; it is usually small. One process per data directory. Scale up (bigger batches, more in-flight batches) rather than out; for isolation, run several installations with their own data directories.

Profiles were taken with go test -tags bench -cpuprofile/-memprofile during the load test: Documents are encoded to NDJSON by a hand-written encoder and sent with the SDK's NDJSON calls: encoding is 3.8× faster with 23× less memory and 13× fewer allocations; the writer's CPU dropped 45% and its allocations 58% end to end. Encode buffers are pooled and pre-sized from the previous batch; retries resend the same bytes. The transform copies nested maps and slices only when something inside needs converting: 27% fewer bytes and 3 fewer allocations per row. argon2id key derivation uses OWASP's 19 MiB / 2-pass profile instead of 64 MiB: 45 MiB less allocated at startup. In total, process CPU dropped 23% (2.26 s to 1.74 s for 250k documents) in the end-to-end test.

The task's state. failed is a configuration problem (fix and start again); retrying is transient and resolves itself; held is a safety guard waiting for you. The task's Logs tab and the error under its status. The service log (journalctl -u meilisearch-cdc, docker logs cdc); set CDC_LOG_LEVEL=debug for more. entries.x: Not an error to fix: the stored position no longer exists on the source (a purged binlog, an invalidated or dropped replication slot, an oplog that rolled over, an expired DynamoDB shard, a trimmed Redis stream, SQL Server change rows removed by cleanup, a position older than CockroachDB's GC window). Does it need Kafka or Debezium? No. Most sources are read directly. Kafka is one optional source, for databases only Debezium supports. Can one table feed several Meilisearch instances? Yes: create one task per destination on the same connector and table. For PostgreSQL each task has its own slot. Can several tables feed one index? Yes, with the same primary key field and the upsert write mode, so each task merges its fields. Static fields help tell sources apart. What delivery guarantee does it give? At-least-once with idempotent writes: a change may be applied twice after a crash, never lost, and applying it twice gives the same document. Can I run two replicas for high availability? No. The state store is single-writer; run one instance and let your orchestrator restart it. Checkpoints make restarts cheap. Does it change my database? Only for PostgreSQL (a replication slot and, unless you name one, a publication per task) and CockroachDB (it may enable kv.rangefeed.enabled if allowed). Deleting a PostgreSQL task with drop source objects removes them. How do I move an installation to another server? Stop it, copy the data directory (with secret.key, or keep the same CDC_SECRET_KEY), start it there. See Backups.

Where to find meilisearch-cdc release notes, Docker image tags and the upgrade checklist and notes to read before moving between versions. Release notes are published with every release on GitHub. This page collects what to check when you upgrade.

GitHub releases: notes generated from the merged changes, the archives for every platform and checksums.txt. Tags look like v1.2.3; pre-releases like v1.3.0-rc.1 are marked as such. ghcr.io/ja7ad/meilisearch-cdc: images tagged 1.2.3, 1.2 and, for final releases, latest.

Read the notes of every release between your version and the target. Back up the data directory and the key. Replace the binary or the image tag, restart, and watch the tasks resume from their checkpoints. Reload open dashboards (installed apps offer Reload by themselves).

Notes that need action from operators will be listed here, newest first. No breaking changes recorded yet Data written by older versions is migrated on start where needed. For example, an installation from before the primary administrator existed gets its oldest admin promoted to owner, and secrets stored in an older encryption format are re-encrypted with the current key.
